title: The New Era of Indian Agriculture and Allied Sectors
subtitle: “Driving Growth, Resilience and Food Security”
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                12 AUG 2026 5:36PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Driving Agricultural Transformation
India’s agriculture and allied sectors are witnessing a significant transformation, marked by rising productivity, stronger farmer support systems, and greater resilience. Agriculture remains the backbone of India's economy, providing livelihoods to approximately
46.1 percent
of the workforce. Livestock and fisheries have maintained stable growth of
5-6 percent
, strengthening rural incomes and supporting agricultural diversification. Over the past decade, sustained policy interventions have improved access to credit, insurance, and markets, and accelerated the adoption of digital technologies. Growing investments in food processing, cooperatives, livestock, dairy, and fisheries are enabling greater value addition, income diversification, and employment across the agricultural value chain.
Strengthening the Agricultural Economy
The GVA of the Agriculture and Allied Sector
increased from
Rs.
20.94 lakh crore
in
2014-15
to an estimated
Rs.
52.08 lakh crore
in
2025-26
.
Budget allocation for the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare increased from
Rs.
27,663 crore in 2013-14
to
Rs.
1,40,528.78 crore in 2026
-
27
.
Harvesting Higher Production
Total foodgrain production increased from
265.05 million tonnes in 2013-14 to 376.56 million tonnes in 2025-26 (Third Advance Estimates).
Horticulture production increased from
280.70 million tonnes in 2013-14 to approximately 377.78 million tonnes in 2025-26 (Second Advance Estimates)
.
Oilseeds production increased from
27.51 million tonnes
in
2014-15
to
43.06 million tonnes
in
2025-26
(
Third Advance Estimates)
.
Securing Farmers' Livelihoods
Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM-KISAN)
More than
Rs.4.47 lakh crore
has been transferred directly into farmers’ bank accounts through
23 instalments
under the Scheme.
Under the 23rd instalment, more
than 9.49 crore farmers benefited
, with over
Rs.18,984 crore
released.
The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY)
Since its launch in 2016-17, over
92.46 crore
farmer applications have been insured.
Claims worth
Rs.1.96 lakh crore
have been disbursed up to December 2025, benefiting around
24.31 crore farmers
.
Minimum Support Prices (MSP)
Total procurement increased from
698.7 million tonnes
during
2004-2014 to 1,229.2 million tonnes
during
2014-2026.
Total MSP value increased from
Rs.
7.41 lakh crore
during 2004-2014 to
Rs.
26.32 lakh crore
during
2014-
2026
(up to February 2026).
MSP for Paddy (Grade A) increased from
Rs.1,400 per quintal in 2014-15 to Rs.2,461 per quintal in 2026-27
.
MSP for Wheat increased from
Rs.1,400 per quintal in 2014-15 to Rs.2,585 per quintal in 2026-27.
The Kisan Credit Card (KCC) scheme
As on 3rd August 2026,
7.28 crore
Kisan Credit Card (KCC) accounts were operational across the country in 2025-26.
The amount outstanding under the Kisan Credit Card (KCC) scheme stood at
Rs.
10.08 lakh crore.
The Pradhan Mantri Kisan Maandhan Yojana (PMKMY)
As of February 2026, around
24.96 lakh farmers
have been enrolled under the scheme.
Towards Sustainable Agriculture
The Soil Health Card (SHC) Scheme
26.09 crore soil health cards
have been issued as of July 2026.
⁠In addition, over
70,002 Krishi Sakhis
have been trained to provide soil health advisories and support informed farm practices.
Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY)
Since its inception (as of June 2026),
18.93 lakh hectares
of area have been covered, benefiting
33.63 lakh
farmers.
Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER)
Since its inception (as on 30 June 2026),
2.36 lakh
hectares
have been brought under organic farming benefitting
2.74 lakh
farmers.
National Mission on Natural Farming (NMNF)
During FY 2025-26,
18,893
clusters covering
10.32 lakh hectares
and involving
20.93 lakh
farmers were formed under the Mission.
33.89 lakh
farmers have been made aware of natural farming.
More than
22.47 lakh
farmers have been registered under the Natural Farming Certification System (NFCS), of which over
14.43 lakh
farmers have been certified.
Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha Evam Utthan Mahabhiyan (PM KUSUM)
As on 2nd August 2026,
Nearly
11.49 lakh off-grid solar pumps
have been installed for agricultural use.
More than
15.89 lakh agricultural pumps
are covered through feeder-level solarisation.
Around
1,726 MW
of decentralized solar power capacity was commissioned on farmers’ land.
Over
21.77 lakh farmers
benefited across the country.
Ensuring Food for All
As of February 2026, under the
National Food Security Act (NFSA),
against the intended coverage of
81.35 crore
, the States/UTs have identified
80.56 crore persons
for the provision of subsidized foodgrains.
Around
79.8 crore beneficiaries
are covered across the country under
NFSA, as of December 2025.
Centre to spend
Rs. 25,530 crore
in next 5 years under
SARTHAK PDS -
Scheme for Assistance in Ration Transport and Handling-Income with Automation in PDS.
The Scheme will work towards fulfilling India's commitment to
81.35 crore
persons covered under NFSA.
Building Stronger Rural Institutions through Cooperatives and FPO
s
10,000 Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs)
have been registered across the country as of July 2026.
79,630 Primary Agricultural Credit Societies
(PACS)
have been sanctioned for computerization across 31 States and Union Territories.
63,707 PACS
have been onboarded on the
Enterprise Resource Planning
(ERP)
based national software as of 05th August 2026.
Connecting Farms to Markets
National Agriculture Market (e-NAM)
As of June 2026,
1,656 mandis
have been integrated.
1.89 crore farmers
and
2.78 lakh traders
have been registered on e-NAM.
Agricultural Marketing Infrastructure (AMI)
As of July 2026,
12,353
storage infrastructure projects with a storage capacity of
369.18 LMT
have been sanctioned in the last ten years.
Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF)
Interest subvention support has been extended to
18,893
warehouses,
3,110
cold stores/cold chain projects and
2,105
integrated primary and secondary processing units.
Food Processing Reforms
Enhanced Financial Support for Food Processing
Budget allocation for the Ministry of Food Processing Industries increased from
Rs.785.86 crore in 2014-15 to
Rs.4,064 crore in 2026-27
.
Production Linked Incentive Scheme for Food Processing Industry (PLISFPI)
Incentives amounting to
Rs.
3,271.44 crore
have been disbursed up to June 2026.
The investments undertaken under the Scheme have resulted in the creation of food processing capacity of
34 lakh metric tonnes per annum.
Sales of PLI-supported products increased from
Rs.
58,758 crore
in FY 2019-20 to
Rs.
1,08,854 crore
in FY 2025-26.
Pradhan Mantri Kisan Sampada Yojna (PMKSY)
As of June 2026,
1,256
projects (post-harvest infrastructure and processing facilities) have been completed or are operational, benefitting about
37.76 lakh
farmers.
294.21 LMT/Annum
of processing and preservation capacity created, generating
9.16 lakh
employment opportunities across the country.
Taking Indian Agriculture Global
The value of agricultural exports increased from
USD 32.08 billion in 2014-15 to USD 54.70 billion in 2025-26
, recording a growth of about
70.5 percent
.
Share of processed food exports increased from
13.7 percent in 2014-15 to 20.4 percent in 2024-25
, a nearly
49 percent rise
.
Technology at the Farmgate
Under the Digital Agriculture Mission
As on 3rd August 2026
More than
10.31 Crore
Farmer IDs have been created across the country. Further, during Rabi 2025-26, the Digital Crop Survey (DCS) was conducted in 648 Districts covering more than
31.3 crore plots
across the country.
AI-Enabled Initiatives:
National Pest Surveillance System (NPSS)-
As of July 2026, this tool is being used by over
10,000
extension workers supporting
73 crops over 436 pests.
BharatVistaar-
As of July 2026, the platform has served over
3 lakh
farmers and addressed more than
72 lakh
farmer queries.
Empowering Farmers Through Knowledge
Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs)
As of June 2026,
The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) has established
731 KVKs
across the country.
Around
58.02 lakh farmers
were trained between 2021-22 and 2023-24.
An additional
18.56 lakh farmers
were trained during the first ten months of 2024-25.
Agricultural Diversification and the Growth of Allied Sectors
Livestock and Dairy as Drivers of Rural Economic Growth
The livestock sector has recorded a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of
12.77 percent
since 2014-15.
In the Union Budget 2026-27,
Rs.
6,153.46 crore
has been allocated to the Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying
.
Indigenous and non-descript cattle productivity
reached
1,343.2 kilograms per animal
per year
in 2024-25 from 927 kilograms per animal per year in 2014-15.
Buffalo productivity
reached
2,365.2 kilograms per animal per year
in 2024-25 from 1880 kilograms per animal per year in 2014-15.
Average bovine milk productivity
has reached
2,251 kilograms per animal per year
in 2024-25 from 1,648 kg per animal per year in 2014-15.
India holds the
leading global position
in
milk production
, accounting for nearly
25 percent of global output.
Per capita milk availability reached
485 grams per day in 2024-25
, compared to the global average of
394 grams per day
.
Milk production has increased by
70 percent
, rising from
146.31 million tonnes
in 2014-15 to
248 million tonnes
in 2024-25.
Poultry and meat production have also expanded, with India ranking
second in egg production and fourth in meat production globally
:
Egg production has grown
by
90 percent
, increasing from
78.48 billion eggs
in 2014-15 to
149.11 billion eggs
in 2024-25.
Per capita egg
availability has risen from
62 eggs per annum
in 2014-15 to
106 eggs per annum
in 2024-25.
Meat Production has increased from
6.69 million tonnes
in 2014-15 to
10.50 million tonnes
in 2024-25.
Strengthening Fisheries Infrastructure, Market Access and Credit Support
The
Union Budget 2026-27
allocated a record
Rs.
2,761.80 crore
to fisheries under the Blue Revolution initiatives.
Fish production reached
197.75 lakh tonnes
in
2024-25, up
from 95.79 lakh tonnes in FY 2013-14.
Seafood exports increased from USD 3.64 billion in 2013-14 to around
USD 8.46 billion
in 2025-26.
Fisheries Infrastructure and Market Access
Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY)
Rs.
2,500 crore
allocated under the Union Budget
2026-27
.
As on April 2026
, Key activities approved:
28,489
fish transportation and handling units
1,394
live fish vending units,
6,018
fish kiosks, and 117 fish retail markets
775
cold storages and ice plants, and 24 wholesale fish markets
Institutional Credit Support for fisheries
6.83 lakh applications
were received under the
Kisan Credit Card (KCC)
,
of which
6.77 lakh
were accepted. Of which,
4.82 lakh applications
were sanctioned
,
indicating a meaningful conversion of demand into credit access as
of early
2026.
KCC benefits have reached
4.39 lakh fishers
. Insurance coverage has been provided to
33 lakh
beneficiaries. An average of
7.44 lakh
fisher families received livelihood assistance during lean fishing periods.
Strengthening Livestock through Infrastructure and Entrepreneurship
National Livestock Mission
As on 4th August 2026,
4,084 breed
multiplication farms
for
poultry, sheep, goat, pig, camel, horse, and donkey have been approved.
1.61 lakh metric tonnes
of quality fodder seed have been produced.
Entrepreneurship Development Programme
under the National Livestock Mission, as on
11th August 2026,
4,321 projects approved
, worth
Rs.
2,948.68 crore
total project cost with the
Rs.
1,386.18 crore
approved subsidy
Animal Husbandry Infrastructure Development Fund (AHIDF)
Projects approved with
418 lakh litres/day
of milk processing capacity and value-addition capacity as on 4th August 2026.
Bharat
Pashudhan
As of 6th August
2026,
Livestock Owners Registered:
9.84 crore
, Pashu Aadhaar Issued:
Over 38.53 crore
, All Vaccinations:
168.67 crore
.
National Programme for Dairy Development (
NPDD)
As on June 2026,
36,611
new Dairy Cooperative Societies have been organised.
34,557
village-level dairy cooperative societies have been strengthened.
168 lakh litres/day
of milk chilling capacity has been created.
76,748
milk quality testing devices have been distributed.
Advancing Livestock Breeding, Productivity, and Animal Health
A total of
47,687 Multi-Purpose Artificial Insemination Technicians in Rural India
(MAITRIs)
have been trained, 24 IVF laboratories established, 48 semen stations sanctioned, and 28 heifer rearing centres approved under RGM as on 4th August 2026.
During the last five years,
over 17.27 crore
artificial inseminations have been carried out under the
Nationwide Artificial Insemination Programme
, benefiting nearly
5.98 crore farmers
.
Accelerated Breed Improvement programme
: As on 4th August 2026, 7,959 embryos transferred, 1,666 pregnancies established, and 1,223 calves born. Out of which 1,142 of the calves are females.
Strengthening Animal Health and Risk Mitigation
Livestock productivity and income stability are closely linked to disease control. Under
National Animal Disease Control Programme (NADCP)
As of March 2026,
132.49 crore
doses of the Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) vaccine have been administered.
Brucellosis Control Programme:
As of March 2026,
3.17 crores
, 4-8 months old bovine female calf for Brucellosis have been vaccinated in the country since inception.
296.74 lakh vaccine doses
administered to eligible female calves to prevent brucellosis and strengthen livestock health during the last five years alone.
Mobile Veterinary Units (MVUs)
4,019 MVUs
are operational across 29 States/UTs, delivering doorstep veterinary services through the toll-free number
1962
as of July 2026.
Benefited
119.77 lakh farmers
and
treated 245.05 lakh animals
, significantly boosting farmer confidence and supporting the livestock sector as a viable enterprise.

title: Affordable and Accessible Healthcare for All
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                12 AUG 2026 5:11PM by PIB Delhi
content:
In past 12 years, the Government of India has significantly strengthened India’s health system. Quality healthcare is
more accessible, more affordable, and more equitable
than it has ever been.  This aligns with the principle of
“Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas and Sabka Prayas”
to build an Atmanirbhar Bharat.
Ayushman Bharat
T
he Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana
(AB-PMJAY)
provides health insurance of Rs. 5 lakh per family per year to families from the poorest 40% of society and all senior citizens aged 70 and above
.
Over
40,000 claims are processed every single day
for over 1,900 treatment packages.
Since the scheme launched in 2018, as of
August 12, 2026:
Over 45.5 crore Ayushman Cards
have been issued
12.69 crore hospitalizations
have been covered, amounting to Rs. 1.92 lakh crore (as on June 30, 2026)
Over
38,466 public and private hospitals
are empanelled
1.20 crore senior citizens
enrolled under the Ayushman Bharat Vay Vandana scheme.
Over 13.84 lakh treatments, worth Rs. 3,000-crore
have been availed.
Under AB PM-JAY, 29.05 lakh inter-state portability hospital admissions, amounting to more than Rs. 8,383.97 crore, have been authorised (as on June 30, 2026)
Over 1.86 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs
(AAMs)
are now functional across the country to provide primary healthcare at every neighbourhood (As of 12 August 2026). These centres offer
12 free services
and have recorded a cumulative footfall of over
540 crore till date
.
The
Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM)
:
Support for 23,224 rural health and wellness centres in 10 high-focus states.
Establishing 13,736 urban health and wellness centres in all states.
3,389 block public health units in 11 high-focus states.
Setting up 744 integrated public health labs in all districts.
Establishing 631 critical care hospital blocks in all districts with a population of more than 5 lakh.
And underpinning all of this is India’s digital health backbone, the
Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM).
Coverage under ABDM (as of August 12, 2026):
96.43 crore ABHA
health identity numbers created
Over 110
crore health records
have been linked with ABHA
Over 5.47 lakh health facilities
have been registered on the platform
More than 10.50 lakh healthcare professionals
have been registered on the platform.
National Health Mission: Targeted Health Interventions
The
National Health Mission (NHM),
with its two sub-missions-
National Rural Health Mission and National Urban Health Mission
, delivers targeted programmes that address specific diseases, populations, and health challenges. NHM has significantly improved public health outcomes across maternal and child health, disease elimination, and immunisation.
Maternal and Child Health: Making Safe Births the Norm
The
Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan
has enabled over
7.91 crore free antenatal check-ups
.
More than 1.24 crore high-risk pregnancies have been identified.
First-trimester antenatal registration in India increased from 58.6% in NFHS-4 (2015-16) to 76.2% in NFHS-6 (2023-24).
Mothers receiving four or more antenatal care visits in India increased significantly from 51.2% in NFHS-4 (2015-16) to 65.2% in NFHS-6 (2023-24).
Institutional deliveries in India increased from 78.9% in NFHS-4 (2015-16) to 90.6% in NFHS-6 (2023-24).
On immunisation, the
Universal Immunisation Programme
reaches
2.67 crore newborns
and
2.9 crore pregnant women every year
with free vaccines against 12 diseases.
Mission Indradhanush
, launched in 2014, has functioned as a catch-up drive, vaccinating
5.46 crore children
and
1.32 crore pregnant women
across its various phases.
The percentage of zero-dose children-those who had received no vaccines at all-dropped from
0.11% of the population in 2023 to 0.06% in 2024
.
Under Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP), the government launched
U-WIN
in October 2024 — a platform that ensures no family loses its vaccination records. As of March 2026,
11.87 crore children
and
3.96 crore pregnant women
are already registered.
In February 2026, the government launched a three-month campaign to provide free
HPV vaccines
to
1.2 crore girls aged 14 years,
for combating cervical cancer.
52,10,302 girls
have received the HPV vaccine across the country (as on July 15, 2026).
These initiatives have improved various mortality rates, including:
Maternal mortality rate
declined to
87 per 1,00,000 live births in 2022-24 from 130 per 1,00,000 in 2014-16
.
Neonatal mortality
rate declined to
17 per 1,000 live births in 2023 from 28 per 1,000 live births in 2015.
Under-5 mortality rate
declined to
28 per 1,000 live births in 2023 from 48 per 1,000 live births in 2015
.
Eliminating Communicable Diseases: Real Progress on Long-Standing Burdens
The government has reduced the prevalence of communicable diseases over the past 12 years.
New cases of tuberculosis emerging yearly in India
dipped by 21% from 2015-2024; mortality due to TB dropped by 28% during the same period
.
Treatment success rates in
Tuberculosis
have climbed from
83% in 2021 to 90% in 2025
— and treatment coverage has gone from
53% (2015) to 92% (2024).
More than
28.1 crore people
have already been
screened
,
20 Lakh people given preventive treatment,
and
5.7 lakh new Nikshay Mitras have been added
so far under the intensified campaigns since December 2024.
Malaria cases and deaths have fallen by
80.5% and 78.38% respectively between 2015 and 2023
. India exited the WHO's 'High Burden to High Impact (HBHI) group' for malaria in 2024.
Non-Communicable Diseases: Catching Problems Early
National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD)
focuses on strengthening infrastructure, human resource development, screening, early diagnosis, referral, treatment, and health promotion for Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs). Through nationwide screening drives:
41.5 crore Screened for hypertension
41.3 crore for diabetes
35.3 crore for oral cancer and
16.5 crore for breast cancer.
The
Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme
(launched 2016) has provided free dialysis to
32.44 lakh patients
across
1,856 centres
(as of June, 2026).
Under the Strengthening of Tertiary Cancer Care Centres Facilities Scheme,
19 State Cancer Institutes (SCIs) and 20 Tertiary Cancer Care Centers (TCCCs) have been approved
.
Under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases,
770 District NCD Clinics, 524 Day Care Cancer Centres (DCCCs) and 6,410 NCD clinics
at Community Health Centres have been set up across the country.
India has achieved a
17.3% relative
reduction in overall tobacco use
from 2009-10 to 2016-17, as per the Report of the second round of the Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS- 2).
To achieve a tobacco-free generation, the Government launched the Tobacco Free Youth Campaign in 2023 — now in its third edition. This work has earned India the
2025 Bloomberg Philanthropies Award
for tobacco control.
Making Medicines and Tests Actually Affordable
The
Pradhan Mantri Bharatiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana
(PMBJP)
has made generic medicines cheaper. The
Jan Aushadhi Kendras,
where these medicines are available, have grown from a handful of stores in 2014-15 to over
18,646 Jan Aushadhi Kendras
as of February 2026.
These medicines are sold at
50–80% below branded prices
, with a basket of over
2,000 medicines and 300 surgical devices
.
AMRIT (Affordable Medicines and Reliable Implants for Treatment) Pharmacies
launched in 2015, go even further, offering life-saving medicines at discounts of
50–90%
, making treatment affordable for low-income patients who would otherwise go without treatment.
The scheme has benefited
more than 6.85 crore patients
and
medicines worth over Rs.
17,000 crore
at MRP have been dispensed so far, resulting in cumulative savings of about Rs. 8,400 crore for patients.
Free Diagnostics Service Initiative
under NHM makes tests, X-rays, blood work free at every level of the public health system from sub-centres all the way up to district hospitals, spanning haematology, radiology, biochemistry, and more.
Diagnostics services are provided free of cost at all levels of public health facilities
14 tests at Sub Centers
63 at Primary Health Centers
97 at Community Health Centres
111 tests at Sub District Hospitals
134 tests at District Hospitals.
Reaching People Where They Are: Digital Health and Telemedicine
eSanjeevani
, India's national telemedicine platform, has delivered over
49 crore consultations
since its launch in 2019 (as on August 11, 2026). Over
2.4 lakh healthcare providers
are now on the platform.
Tele-MANAS
— launched in October 2022 — was introduced as a toll-free helpline (14416) available nationwide, offering a wide range of mental health services.
It operates in
20 languages
across all 36 states and union territories. It has already received
43.64 lakh calls
since the launch of the service, through 53 Tele-Manas Cells and 23 Mentoring Institutes (as on August 11, 2026).
i-DRONE
service launched in 2021 is delivering medicines and vaccines by drone.
22,000 medicines
have been delivered over
7,700 kilometres
through 65 healthcare centres.
AI is now also embedded in care delivery. Between April 2023 and November 2025,
28.2 crore eSanjeevani consultations
were supported by AI-enabled Clinical Decision Support Systems, providing real-time clinical alerts to doctors.
Building the Workforce India Needs
Over the past 12 years, the number of medical colleges has
more than doubled
— from 387 to
818 allopathy colleges (as of 2025-2026)
.
12 new AIIMS
have been made functional since 2014. There are 23 AIIMS now.
MBBS and PG seats
increased to 1,28,976 and 85,822, respectively, as of 2025-26.
Nursing has received equal attention.
157 new nursing colleges
are being set up, adding around
15,700 nursing graduates annually
.
B.Sc. Nursing seats are up
53%
to 1,27,290, and M.Sc. Nursing seats up
39%
to 14,986 as of June 2025.
Alternative Healthcare
Alongside modern medicine, the government has formally integrated traditional healthcare systems into the public health framework. The
Ministry of AYUSH
(Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa Rigpa, and Homeopathy), formed in November 2014, has established traditional medicines as an active part of India's health system.
942 AYUSH institutions
exist in the country as of May 2025.
Ayush Grid is India’s digital bridge between traditional healing and modern healthcare delivery, making AYUSH more accessible, integrated, and future-ready. This AYUSH Grid will digitally connect all AYUSH hospitals and laboratories nationwide.

title: Financial Inclusion in India: Banking Every Citizen, Empowering Every Household
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                12 AUG 2026 4:16PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Introduction
Financial inclusion is central to India's vision of equitable development. Over the past decade, India has expanded access to banking, digital payments, credit, insurance, pensions and investment opportunities. Digital Public Infrastructure and citizen-centric reforms have driven this transformation. India has moved beyond universal bank account ownership towards active participation in the formal financial system. This transformation has empowered millions of households, entrepreneurs and businesses.
Key Indicators of Financial Inclusion in India
Several indicators highlight the significant progress made in expanding financial access, infrastructure and participation across India.
RBI's Financial Inclusion (FI) Index
The
RBI's FI Index
measures the extent of financial inclusion across access, usage and quality of financial services. It serves as a comprehensive indicator of progress in expanding formal financial services nationwide. The FI Index increased from
43.4 in March 2017
to
70.0 in March 2026
, reflecting broad-based improvements across all three dimensions.
World Bank Global Findex
The Global Findex Database is the world's leading source of data on financial inclusion. It measures how adults access and use financial services across economies. The
Global Findex 2025
highlights India's remarkable progress in financial inclusion.
Account ownership has reached 89%
since 2011, reflecting significant gains in access to formal financial services and active account usage over the past decade.
Banking Access Network
Bank branches remain the foundation of India's formal banking system. They provide savings, credit and other financial services across the country. India has
over 1.81 lakh bank branches
(17 July 2026).
Banking access is delivered through branches, Business Correspondents and India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) outlets. As of
6 March 2026
,
99.92% villages in the country
are covered with banking outlets within a 5 km radius.
IPPB strengthens last-mile banking through
over 1.65 lakh post offices
(17 July, 2026). It serves
more than 11 crore customers
across
5.57 lakh villages and towns
.
Business Correspondents extend doorstep banking services to unbanked and under-banked areas. India has
over 17.36 lakh
BC
supporting doorstep banking services nationwide (17 July 2026).
Pillars of Financial Inclusion
India's financial inclusion ecosystem rests on interconnected policy and institutional pillars. They promote universal access and meaningful participation in the formal financial system.
Universal Banking
Pradhan Mantri Jan - Dhan Yojana (PMJDY)
PMJDY (2014)
provides every unbanked adult with a basic savings bank account
where minimum balance needs to be maintained.
It offers access to savings, remittances, credit, insurance, pension and Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT).
PMJDY account holders are provided a RuPay Debit Card and accident insurance cover. The insurance cover is ₹2 lakh for accounts opened after 28 August 2018 and ₹1 lakh for accounts opened before that date. Eligible account holders can also avail an overdraft facility up to ₹10,000.
It facilitates enrolment under Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY), Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY), Atal Pension Yojana (APY), and access to MUDRA loans.
JAM Trinity
The
JAM Trinity
Integrates Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar and mobile connectivity
to strengthen financial inclusion.
It
enables Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)
for transparent and efficient delivery of government benefits. DBT
reduces leakages, eliminates fake beneficiaries and minimises intermediaries
in welfare delivery.
The JAM Trinity
strengthens formal banking access
and promotes trust in digital financial services.

From Access to Empowerment
India's financial inclusion journey has evolved from expanding account ownership to enabling meaningful financial participation. A strong network of banks, digital infrastructure and government schemes has widened access to formal financial services. PMJDY, JAM trinity, social security and inclusive credit have strengthened financial resilience across diverse sections of society.  Digital payments and financial literacy are further enabling citizens to participate confidently in the formal financial system. Together, these initiatives are building a more accessible, resilient and inclusive financial ecosystem that supports inclusive growth.

title: Reforming India’s Tribunal System
subtitle: Tribunal Reforms Bill, 2026
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                12 AUG 2026 2:29PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026 seeks to create a more independent, transparent and professionally administered tribunal system. The Bill provides for setting up of a judiciary-led  National Tribunals Commission that will make selections to the tribunals and exercise oversight on their functioning.  The aim is to reduce executive discretion while strengthening accountability. By creating a common institutional framework for tribunal administration, the Bill seeks to address longstanding concerns over appointments, tenure and functioning, while giving effect to the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in its Madras Bar Association judgments.
Strengthening India’s Tribunal System
The Tribunal Reforms Bill, 2026 passed by the Parliament in August 2026, aims to reform the tribunal system to make it more
efficient, independent of the executive, transparent and uniform.
The Bill follows various Supreme Court judgements on the independence of tribunals. In
Madras Bar Association v. Union of India
[(2026) 2 SCC 1], the Supreme Court struck down provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021. The Court also directed the establishment of an independent National Tribunals Commission.
The
2026 Bill proposes to repeal the Tribunal Reforms Act, 2021
. It introduces a new structure to ensure that the system is independent yet accountable to the people it serves.
Covered Tribunals & Governing Acts
The Bill lists all the
Tribunals, Appellate Tribunals, and Authorities
governed by the bill, alongside their corresponding
Enactments
. The changes proposed by the Bill shall apply to these tribunals.
Sl. No.
Tribunal / Appellate Tribunal / Authority
Enactments
1.
Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal
The Customs Act, 1962 (52 of 1962)
2.
Appellate Tribunal
The Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976 (13 of 1976)
3.
Central Administrative Tribunal
The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 (13 of 1985)
4.
State Administrative Tribunals
The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 (13 of 1985)
5.
Railway Claims Tribunal
The Railway Claims Tribunal Act, 1987 (54 of 1987)
6.
Securities Appellate Tribunal
The Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 (15 of 1992)
7.
Debts Recovery Tribunal
The Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 (51 of 1993)
8.
Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal
The Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 (51 of 1993)
9.
Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India Act, 1997 (24 of 1997)
10.
Appellate Tribunal for Electricity
The Electricity Act, 2003 (36 of 2003)
11.
Armed Forces Tribunal
The Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007 (55 of 2007)
12.
National Green Tribunal
The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 (19 of 2010)
13.

The Companies Act, 2013 (18 of 2013)
14.

The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (35 of 2019)
15.
Industrial Tribunal constituted by the Central Government
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (35 of 2020)
16.
Income-tax Appellate Tribunal
The Income-tax Act, 2025 (30 of 2025)
A New National Tribunals Commission
The 2026 Bill aims at protecting the independence of the tribunals system through the establishment of a new
National Tribunals Commission (NTC)
. This commission, which will be
dominated by the high-ranking members of the judiciary
, replaces the Central Government, which was given the charge of making key appointments and services conditions according to the Tribunal Reforms Act, 2021.
Composition of the Commission
The Commission would consist of:
A Chairperson
who has been a Judge of the Supreme Court or a Chief Justice of a High Court, and
Four Members:
Two shall be Judicial Members
who have been Chief Justice or Judge of a High Court
Two shall be Technical Members with
at least 25 years of experience in the fields of public administration, finance, law, accountancy, banking, management, or technology.
The Central Government will formally appoint the Chairperson and the Judicial Members of the Commission. However, it must consult the Chief Justice of India before appointing the Chairperson and Judicial Members.
Functions of the Commission
Under the
Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026
, the National Tribunals Commission (NTC) has several important roles:
Conduct selections:
Conduct the selection process for filling up the vacancies of Chairpersons and Members of the Tribunals through Search-cum-Selection Committees.
Review performance:
Monitor tribunal performance and prepares annual reports to be submitted to the Central Government.
Oversee inquiries:
Supervise inquiries into complaints against tribunal members.
Maintain data:
Develops and maintains the National Tribunals Data Grid, which is a portal containing the repository of all case-related information pertaining to the 16 tribunals.
Term of Service
The Chairperson of the Commission or a Member of the Commission shall hold office for a term of five years or till he attains the age of seventy years, whichever is earlier
A Member of a Tribunal shall hold office for a term of five years or till he attains the age of sixty-seven years, whichever is earlier.
The framework also allows reappointment, with previous service and performance considered during the selection process.
New Secretariat
The
Secretariat
serves as the administrative support system for the National Tribunals Commission. The Secretariat will be headed by a Secretary to the Government of India. Its other officers and employees, including their number and service conditions, will be prescribed by rules. It will function under the general and administrative oversight of the Commission’s Chairperson. It:
Empanels experts:
Identifies and empanels experts from relevant fields to assess candidates.
Communicates recommendations:
Sends the Search-cum-Selection Committee’s recommendations to the Central Government within
three days
.
Provides administrative support:
Supports the Commission and carries out functions prescribed.
Prepares annual reports:
Prepares an annual report yearly giving full and true account of the activities of the Commission and forward the report to the Central government.
Search-cum-Selection Committees
The selection of Chairpersons and Members to various tribunals will be done through
Search-cum-Selection Committees.
These committees will be responsible for evaluating candidates and recommending appointments to tribunal posts.
Under
Section 13 of the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026
, the Search-cum-Selection Committee comprises:
For selecting a Tribunal Chairperson
Chairperson of the National Tribunals Commission
Technical Member of the Commission
Retired Chief Justice of a High Court
, nominated by the Commission Chairperson
Secretary to the Government of India
, nominated by the Central Government. In case of appointment to the post of Chairperson of the State Administrative Tribunals, the Chief Secretary to the State Government concerned shall be the Member
Two empanelled experts
who assessed the candidates
Secretary of the Commission
— Member Secretary
For selecting a Tribunal Member:
Judicial Member of the National Tribunals Commission
— Committee Chair
Technical Member of the Commission
Retired High Court Judge
, nominated by the Commission Chairperson
Secretary to the Government of India
, nominated by the Central Government.  In case of appointment to the post of Member of the State Administrative Tribunals, the Chief Secretary to the State Government concerned shall be the Member
Two empanelled experts
who assessed the candidates
Secretary of the Commission
— Member Secretary
The Committee Chair has the
casting vote
, while the
Member Secretary and expert Members do not have voting rights
. The Committee:
Selects candidates:
Conducts the selection process for Chairpersons and Members.
Recommends candidates:
The Committee recommends
one suitable candidate for each vacancy
and one additional candidate for the waiting list.
Considers past performance:
For candidates seeking reappointment, the Committee considers their previous service and performance.
Facilitates timely appointments:
Recommendations are sent to the Central Government through the Secretariat, which must communicate them within
three days
. The Government must process the recommendation and make the appointment within
three months
.
The proposed National Tribunals Commission has a judicial majority. Its Search-cum-Selection Committees are also judicially chaired. The judicial Chairperson has the casting vote. The Committee recommends a single candidate rather than a panel of names. This strengthens judicial influence over the selection process while limiting executive discretion.
Financial and Administrative Independence
The Bill seeks to give tribunals greater financial and administrative autonomy. Under this framework, individual tribunals will identify their requirements for funds, staff, and premises. The Commission's Secretariat will consolidate these projections, and the Commission will evaluate them using an objective framework to determine overall allocation needs.
The Central Government will continue to allocate the necessary grants following parliamentary appropriation.To ensure financial accountability and transparency, the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India (CAG) will audit the accounts of the Commission and forward the audit report to the Central Government, which will then lay it before both Houses of Parliament.
Towards a More Independent Tribunal System
The
Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026
seeks to establish judicial independence and transparency in the tribunals system. While the Bill reinforces judicial independence, it balances this by keeping the system accountable to the public through parliamentary oversight.
The proposed National Tribunals Commission creates a permanent institutional mechanism for appointments, performance review and disciplinary oversight. Judicially led selection committees strengthen the judicial element in appointments. Expert assessment places greater emphasis on professional competence. Five-year tenure provides greater stability.
The Bill marks a shift from fragmented, executive-driven tribunal rules to a structured institutional framework. Its core goal is to establish a more independent, transparent, and professionally managed system that aligns with the Supreme Court's Madras Bar Association jurisprudence.

title: World Elephant Day
subtitle: Celebrating Elephants, Ecosystems and Coexistence
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                12 AUG 2026 11:27AM by PIB Delhi
content:
World Elephant Day highlights the ecological and cultural importance of elephants. India hosts nearly 60% of the world’s wild Asian elephant population and has strengthened conservation through Project Elephant, Elephant Reserves and protected corridors. Scientific monitoring, technology-driven conservation and community participation further support coexistence between people and elephants. These sustained efforts reflect the Government of India’s commitment to safeguarding elephants, ecosystems and India’s natural heritage.
The Gentle Giant of India's Forests
India is home to nearly
60% of the world’s wild Asian elephants
, highlighting its vital role in global elephant conservation. Elephants hold deep cultural significance and play a vital role in healthy ecosystems. As a keystone species, they sustain forests, support biodiversity and maintain ecological balance. The
Synchronous All India Population Estimation of Elephants (SAIEE) 2021–25
estimates India’s wild elephant population at
22,446
. These elephants are protected across
33 Elephant Reserves and 150 identified corridors
.
This rich elephant heritage also brings a responsibility to address growing conservation challenges.
World Elephant Day, observed annually on 12 August
, highlights the need for sustained global action. India’s conservation efforts address habitat loss, fragmentation, poaching, illegal wildlife trade and human-elephant conflict. The country combines
legal protection, habitat conservation, scientific monitoring and community participation
as part of its conservation efforts. Technology-driven measures further strengthen these efforts and support the long-term survival of elephants in the wild.
The Enduring Significance of Elephants in India
Elephants are integral to India’s natural and cultural heritage
.
Their significance spans ecosystem health, cultural traditions and community identities.
Ecological Importance
Elephants are
foundational species
that shape forest structure and ecosystem functioning. They are migratory in nature, with home ranges spanning
100–3,000 km².
As they move long distances, they create
pathways and water holes that benefit other wildlife.
Their feeding habits support nutrient cycling, and bring about  seed dispersal that aids forest regeneration. This helps in connecting fragmented forests and creating favourable conditions for thriving genetic diversity. Protecting elephants therefore strengthens ecological connectivity, forest health and wider biodiversity.
Cultural and Social Importance
Elephants have shaped India’s religious traditions, cultural practices and community identities for centuries. Lord Ganesha represents wisdom and the removal of obstacles in
North Indian traditions.
Elephants historically symbolised authority and prestige as
royal emblems
. Temple elephants remain part of religious rituals and festivals in
South India
. Communities across the
Northeast
worship Lord Ganesha as a manifestation of their deities and regard elephants with deep respect. Some communities traditionally view elephants as elders and symbols of wisdom. These traditions highlight the enduring place of elephants in India’s cultural heritage and community life.
Counting the Giants: Where India's Elephants Stand Today
India's elephant conservation story is best told through numbers. From reserve networks to corridor restoration, each figure reflects decades of sustained institutional effort.
Project Elephant: A Comprehensive Conservation Framework
Project Elephant
is the Government of India's flagship initiative for elephant conservation. Implemented by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), the programme provides financial and technical support to States for protecting elephant habitats, conserving captive elephants and mitigating human-elephant conflict. It also promotes science-driven conservation through AI-enabled monitoring, radio-collaring, genetic databases and early warning systems.
DNA-based Sampling
Scientific monitoring under Project Elephant has strengthened elephant population assessment. SAIEE 2021–25 used India’s first DNA-based synchronised elephant census. Scientists analysed dung samples to identify individual elephants through unique genetic fingerprints. This helped detect repeat samples across landscapes and improve population estimates. SAIEE combined DNA profiling, block counts and line-transect surveys, strengthening the scientific rigour of elephant population assessment.
Securing India's Elephant Corridors
Elephant corridors play an important role in elephant conservation in India. They connect erstwhile natural habitats that have got fragmented due to human development or other reasons. The elephant corridors are habitats that have been developed to connect fragmented habitats. They are essential for maintaining healthy and genetically diverse elephant populations by enabling safe movement between fragmented habitats and helping reduce human-elephant conflict. They also support long-term population viability by maintaining ecological connectivity. Under
Project Elephant
, the Government has identified and validated elephant corridors across
1
4
elephant-range states
.
According to
Elephant Corridors of India, 2023
, prepared with technical support from the
Wildlife Institute of India
, these
corridors
span across four regions. The
East-Central region
has 52 corridors, followed by the
North-East (48)
,
Southern (32)
and
Northern (18)
regions.
West Bengal
has the highest number, with
26 corridors
. This accounts for more than
17% of the national total
. The network includes
19 inter-state corridors
and
six transboundary corridors
connecting India and Nepal. Monitoring shows increased elephant use in
59 corridors (40%)
, stable use in
29 (19%)
, declining use in
29 (19%)
, and impaired conditions in
15 corridors
.
Protecting these corridors strengthens habitat connectivity, reduces conflict and supports the long-term conservation of India’s elephant populations.
Sustained Corridor Conservation
The Government continues to strengthen these ecological lifelines through scientific monitoring, boundary delineation and integration into State working and management plans. Currently, 150 corridors support elephant movement. These sustained efforts are strengthening habitat connectivity and securing safer movement for elephants across India's forest landscapes.
Growing the Reserve Network
Elephant Reserves
have expanded steadily
since 2014, now covering 80,777 km
across
14 major elephant-range states.
The expansion has brought an additional 8,610 km² under protection, securing critical habitats and strengthening ecological connectivity. It has also improved scientific management and created a stronger foundation for the long-term survival of India's wild elephant population.
Collectively,
Project Elephant
, scientific population estimation, protected reserves and connected corridors have transformed elephant conservation into an integrated landscape-level programme. These initiatives demonstrate the Government's commitment to combining traditional conservation values with modern science to secure the future of the Asian elephant.
Beyond the Count: Protecting Every Elephant
Estimating elephant populations is only one part of conservation. Long-term success depends on safer habitats, stronger legal safeguards and peaceful coexistence with communities. The Government of India has adopted a comprehensive conservation approach that combines science, technology, infrastructure and public welfare. These initiatives protect elephants both inside forests and across shared landscapes.
India has sought to improve how elephant landscapes are managed. The
Management
Effectiveness
Evaluation
framework
for Elephant Reserves was launched in 2023 and tested in four representative reserves—Shivalik, Kaziranga–Karbi Anglong, Mayurbhanj and Nilgiri. Building on the pilot experience, the Government is taking this framework to Elephant Reserves across the country, supported through CAMPA funding. This institutionalises transparent assessment and adaptive management based on measurable conservation outcomes.
More recently, the Ministry has taken this landscape-based approach a step further by developing
Regional
Action
Plans
for all elephant-bearing regions of the country. These plans recognise that elephants range across State boundaries and that challenges relating to habitat connectivity, human-elephant conflict and landscape management require coordinated action across jurisdictions. The Regional Action Plans provide a common framework for States to undertake priority conservation and conflict-mitigation interventions at the landscape scale.
Making Railways Safer for Elephants
The Government has taken decisive steps to reduce elephant deaths along railway corridors. Joint surveys covered
127 sensitive railway stretches
spanning
3,452.4 km
. Further, Seventy-seven stretches across 14 States, covering 1,965.2 km, have been recommended for mitigation measures involving 705 structures, including underpasses, overpasses, ramps, level crossings and bridge modifications. These structural interventions are being complemented by technologies such as optical-fibre-based intrusion detection, seismic sensors and thermal cameras.
Also, AI-enabled
Distributed Acoustic Sensing
systems now provide real-time alerts to loco pilots, station masters and control rooms. Every train collision involving elephants is jointly investigated with the concerned State Forest Department. These sustained interventions reduced train-hit elephant deaths from
26 in 2013
to
12 in 2024
, a decline of more than
50 percent
.
Guarding Captive Elephants Through Genetics
The Government has strengthened safeguards against the illegal trade and movement of captive elephants through science-based monitoring. Under the
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972
, cases related to sale, transport and procurement are referred to State Chief Wildlife Wardens for action. The
Gajah Suchana
mobile application has created a national genetic database containing DNA profiles, morphological characteristics and ownership details of every registered captive elephant. The database verifies identity before movement and provides reliable forensic evidence during legal proceedings.
Captive Elephant (Transfer or Transport) Rules, 2024
To regulate the movement of captive elephants, the Government notified the Captive Elephant (Transfer or Transport) Rules, 2024. A High-Powered Committee examines interstate transfers of captive elephants. It was constituted under the Supreme Court's order dated March 3, 2023. Together, the application, the rules and the committee strengthen transparency and curb illegal transfer of captive elephants.
Supporting Communities for Peaceful Coexistence
Conservation succeeds when communities become equal partners in protecting wildlife. The Government provides ex-gratia assistance under the Centrally Sponsored Schemes
Project Tiger and Elephant
and
Development of Wildlife Habitats
. Assistance includes
₹10 lakh
for death or permanent incapacitation,
₹2 lakh
for grievous injury, treatment costs up to
₹25,000
for minor injuries, and compensation for crop and property losses as per State and UT norms.
The Government has further strengthened conflict management through the
Human-Wildlife Conflict Advisory
. It recommends hotspot mapping, rapid response teams, State and district-level review committees and faster compensation.
Elephant-specific conflict mitigation guidelines
, issued in
2023
, further improve coordination among stakeholders. Together, these measures protect both elephants and people, strengthening safe and sustainable coexistence across India's elephant landscapes.
Reverence to Responsibility
India’s relationship with elephants reflects a unique harmony between
civilisational values and modern conservation
. Revered for centuries, elephants continue to inspire India’s commitment to protecting nature and maintaining ecological balance. This legacy is now strengthened through
scientific research, technology, strong institutions and community participation
.
The Government of India has developed a comprehensive framework for elephant conservation. Efforts include securing habitats, expanding Elephant Reserves, protecting corridors, improving railway safety and regulating captive elephant movement. Support for communities affected by human-elephant conflict further strengthens
coexistence between people and wildlife
.
As India observes
World Elephant Day 2026
, its commitment to elephant conservation remains steadfast. Every protected habitat, restored corridor and community partnership strengthens the future of the Asian elephant. Under
Viksit Bharat
, India continues to protect both its
natural heritage and civilisational legacy
for future generations.
